newsitem.title: USA: American Airlines, others suffer as strike looms.
newsitem.headline: American Airlines, others suffer as strike looms.

text.p: With American Airlines facing a possible strike by pilots this weekend, many of its customers were abandoning the carrier and scores of businesses were preparing for lean times ahead.
The pilots say they will strike just after midnight on Friday unless last-ditch negotiations with the nation's second-biggest airline bring a new four-year labour contract.
There was no sign of progress at talks in Washington Wednesday as pilot union leaders rejected the airline's latest wage proposal, dismissing it as worse than previous offers.

A strike would disrupt plans for hundreds of thousands of travelers over the long President's Day holiday weekend and beyond, and cost American about $30 million a day, according to industry analysts.
Some losses were already kicking in as customers looked elsewhere for leisure and business trips.

"They are probably losing about 90 percent of their business for the weeks ahead," said Lisa Mahjoub, an agent with the White Heron Travel Service in Dallas. "I haven't booked hardly anyone on American in the next three to four weeks. Nobody wants it."

For passengers who already have tickets with American, most travel agents are urging them to make back-up plans with other carriers just in case American is unable to rebook them on competitors' flights.

Royal Caribbean Cruise Lines, one of American's largest customers, has already rebooked about 10,000 of its air-sea packages away from the carrier for the next two weekends and is ignoring American as it books flights for cruise passengers for coming weeks.

"We are looking at the possibility of this going into March and we just can't take chances," said spokesman Rich Steck, adding that Royal Caribbean rebooked the 10,000 flights at its own expense. "It has cost us a bundle already."

The United States Postal Service also dumped American Wednesday, moving business to other carriers as part of its own plannig for a possible strike. American is currently the third-largest air carrier for the Postal Service, moving about 1.5 million pounds of mail a day.
There was minimal activity Wednesday at the American Airlines home base reservations desk at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport.

American Airlines, owned by Fort Worth, Texas-based AMR Corp., carries about 200,000 passengers a day on 2,200 worldwide flights. A strike would cause the most problems in Dallas, Chicago, Los Angeles, Miami, New York and San Juan, Puerto Rico, where the carrier has a large share of traffic.

AMR spokesman Tim Smith said the company's commuter carrier American Eagle would also shut down and that the vast majority of AMR's 90,000 employees would be placed on unpaid "emergency leave" as soon as a strike begins.
But he said reservation agents would work around the clock to help place "as many passengers as we can" onto flights with other carriers.
The threat of the job furloughs has raised tensions inside the airline with pilots reporting threats from other workers, and is also hurting tourism and service companies linked to the airline.

Businesses ranging from luxury Caribbean hotels to taxi cab firms and airport shoeshine stands say they will suffer job losses and a sharp drop in revenues. The airline estimates a 60-day strike would cost the U.S. economy about $5 billion.
Dallas-based catering firm LSG/Sky Chefs Inc. said it plans to put at least a quarter of its 16,000 employees on emergency leave if American is shut down by a strike.
"It would be a very serious blow to us. American represents about one-third of our overall revenues so a strike would have a terrible impact on us and our employees," spokesman Marty Heires said.
Both American and the pilots' union say they want to reach a new contract agreement in Washington this week but concede that serious differences remain.
The airline has unsuccessfully urged union leaders to accept binding arbitration in the dispute and is pushing Congress and the White House to throw their support behind such a solution.
The pilots say the contract dispute has gone on for over two years and that they want a deal now, even if it means a strike.
